tips: Lay the three branches out as (share x rate) products before adding: 0.054, 0.060, 0.006. The sum is the overall rate.
Work in per-cent-of-a-per-cent to avoid decimal slips: 54 + 60 + 6 = 120 ten-thousandths, i.e. 0.0120 x 10 = 0.12.
Sanity bound: the answer must lie between the smallest rate (6%) and the largest (20%). Only 0.12 does - options (a) and (b) are individual branch products.
Option (b) 0.054 is the Agency-1 branch alone and option (a) 0.006 the Agency-3 branch - both punish stopping before the addition.
solution: Let A1, A2, A3 be the events that a car comes from Agency-1, 2 and 3, with P(A1) = 0.6, P(A2) = 0.3, P(A3) = 0.1.
Let C be the event that the car needs an oil change, with P(C|A1) = 0.09, P(C|A2) = 0.20, P(C|A3) = 0.06.
By the law of total probability, P(C) = P(A1)P(C|A1) + P(A2)P(C|A2) + P(A3)P(C|A3).
Hence the probability is 0.12, option (d).

2023-Q2.shortcut: Y given X = x is uniform on (x-1, x+1), whose mean is the midpoint x. So E(Y|X) = X and E[E^2(Y|X)] = E(X^2) = 1.
tips: The mean of U(a,b) is the midpoint (a+b)/2; here ((x-1) + (x+1))/2 = x exactly, so the conditional mean is X itself.
Read the notation carefully: E^2(Y|X) means the SQUARE of the conditional mean, not the second conditional moment.
For X ~ N(0,1), E(X^2) = Var(X) + [E(X)]^2 = 1 + 0 = 1 - the whole answer once the conditional mean is identified.
The half-width 1 of the uniform affects the conditional VARIANCE (1/3) but not the conditional mean, so it never enters this calculation.
solution: Given X = x, the variable Y is uniform on the interval (x - 1, x + 1).
The mean of a uniform distribution is the midpoint of its range, so E(Y | X = x) = ((x-1) + (x+1))/2 = x.
Hence E(Y | X) = X as a random variable.
Therefore E^2(Y|X) = X^2, and E[E^2(Y|X)] = E(X^2).
Hence the value is 1, option (a).

2023-Q3.shortcut: Only statement 1 holds: Var/Mean = 1/theta, so the variance exceeds the mean exactly when theta < 1. The minimum of exponentials is exponential, not chi-square, and memorylessness holds for every theta.
tips: Exponential(theta) with theta as RATE: mean 1/theta, variance 1/theta^2, so the ratio is 1/theta and the comparison reduces to theta versus 1.
Minimum of n i.i.d. Exp(theta) is Exp(n theta) - the exponential family is closed under minima, which is the standard result statement 2 misquotes.
Memorylessness is a property of the exponential FAMILY, holding for every rate parameter; no condition on theta is needed, so statement 3 is false.
The chi-square link that does exist is Exp(1/2) = chi-square(2) - a special case, not a statement about minima.
solution: For X ~ Exponential with rate theta, the mean is 1/theta and the variance is 1/theta^2.
Statement 1: Var/Mean = (1/theta^2)/(1/theta) = 1/theta, which exceeds 1 exactly when theta < 1. So the variance exceeds the mean for 0 < theta < 1. TRUE.
Statement 2: for a sample of n i.i.d. Exponential(theta) variables, P(min > x) = e^(-n theta x), so the minimum is Exponential(n theta), not chi-square. FALSE.

Statement 3: the lack-of-memory property P(X > s+t | X > s) = P(X > t) follows from e^(-theta(s+t))/e^(-theta s) = e^(-theta t), which holds for every theta > 0. No restriction to theta > 1 exists. FALSE.
Only statement 1 is correct.
Hence option (a) is correct.

2023-Q4.shortcut: Rewrite the pmf as C(10,x)(2/5)^x (3/5)^(10-x): a Binomial(10, 0.4). Mean = 4 and variance = 10(0.4)(0.6) = 2.4.
tips: Divide the 5^10 into the two factors: 2^x/5^x = (2/5)^x and 3^(10-x)/5^(10-x) = (3/5)^(10-x). The binomial form then appears immediately.
Read off n = 10 and p = 2/5 = 0.4, giving q = 0.6. Everything else is two multiplications.
For a binomial the variance npq is always LESS than the mean np, since q < 1 - that ordering alone eliminates options (a) and (b).
Mean 4 and variance 2.4 in that order; option (b) 2.4, 4 reverses them, the classic careless-reading trap.
solution: Split the denominator: 5^10 = 5^x . 5^(10-x), so P(X = x) = C(10,x)(2/5)^x (3/5)^(10-x).
This is exactly the Binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 2/5 = 0.4, so q = 0.6.
Hence the mean and variance are 4 and 2.4, option (c).

2023-Q5.shortcut: log(Y/sigma) = mu log X = mu W with W ~ N(mu, sigma^2), so the bracket is mu(W - mu) = mu sigma Z. Its square is mu^2 sigma^2 Z^2 and Var(Z^2) = 2, giving 2 mu^4 sigma^4.
tips: Peel the transformation one layer at a time: Y = sigma X^mu gives Y/sigma = X^mu, so log(Y/sigma) = mu log X - the sigma cancels by design.
X lognormal means W = log X ~ N(mu, sigma^2), so mu W - mu^2 = mu(W - mu), a centred normal with SD mu sigma.
The square of a centred normal is (mu sigma)^2 times a chi-square(1), and Var(chi-square(1)) = 2 - the source of the factor 2.
The distractors encode wrong chi-square variances: 3 (option c) and 15 or 105 (options b, a) come from higher moments of the normal, so pinning Var(Z^2) = 2 is decisive.
solution: X is lognormal(mu, sigma^2), so W = log X follows N(mu, sigma^2).
Y = sigma X^mu gives Y/sigma = X^mu, hence log(Y/sigma) = mu log X = mu W.
Therefore log(Y/sigma) - mu^2 = mu W - mu^2 = mu(W - mu).
Write W - mu = sigma Z with Z ~ N(0,1). Then the bracket is mu sigma Z and its square is mu^2 sigma^2 Z^2.
Since Z^2 ~ chi-square with 1 degree of freedom, Var(Z^2) = 2.
Hence Var(mu^2 sigma^2 Z^2) = mu^4 sigma^4 Var(Z^2) = 2 mu^4 sigma^4, option (d).

2023-Q6.shortcut: The density is Uniform(0,5), so every probability is (interval length)/5. All four values - 0.2, 0.3, 0.6 and 0.8 - check out.
tips: A constant density 0.2 over a range of length 5 is U(0,5); probabilities are then just lengths divided by 5, with no integration at all.
Statement 3 has the trap: |X| >= 2 looks two-sided, but X is confined to [0,5], so it reduces to X >= 2 and gives 3/5 = 0.6.
When every statement in a set is a straightforward computation from the same simple density, expect 'all four' - but verify the one with the absolute value.
solution: The density is f(x) = 0.2 on [0,5], which is the Uniform(0,5) distribution; probabilities equal interval length divided by 5.
Statement 1: P(2 <= X <= 3) = (3 - 2)/5 = 0.2. CORRECT.
Statement 3: since X takes only non-negative values, |X| >= 2 is the same as X >= 2, giving (5 - 2)/5 = 0.6. CORRECT.
Statement 4: P(X < 4) = (4 - 0)/5 = 0.8. CORRECT.
All four probabilities are correct, option (d).

2023-Q7.shortcut: Unit area means pi r^2 = 1, so r^2 = 1/pi. The integral is P(X^2 + Y^2 <= r^2) with X^2+Y^2 ~ chi-square(2) = Exp(1/2), giving 1 - e^(-r^2/2) = 1 - e^(-1/(2 pi)).
tips: 'Unit AREA' not unit radius - solve pi r^2 = 1 first to get r^2 = 1/pi. Reading it as r = 1 leads straight to option (c).
For independent standard normals, X^2 + Y^2 ~ chi-square with 2 d.f., which is Exponential with rate 1/2 - a fact worth memorising.
Hence P(X^2+Y^2 <= c) = 1 - e^(-c/2) for any c > 0; substituting c = 1/pi gives the answer in one step.
The bivariate standard normal density is circularly symmetric, which is precisely why a circular region turns a double integral into a one-dimensional chi-square probability.
solution: The integrand phi(x)phi(y) is the joint density of two independent standard normal variables, so the integral is P((X,Y) lies in A).
A is a circle centred at the origin with unit AREA, so pi r^2 = 1 and r^2 = 1/pi.
The event is therefore X^2 + Y^2 <= r^2 = 1/pi.
For independent standard normals, X^2 + Y^2 follows a chi-square distribution with 2 degrees of freedom, which is exponential with rate 1/2.
Hence P(X^2 + Y^2 <= c) = 1 - e^(-c/2), and with c = 1/pi this is 1 - e^(-1/(2 pi)).
Option (b) is correct.

2023-Q8.shortcut: The density says X | Y = y ~ N(12y, y), and integrating out x leaves f_Y(y) = 1 on (0,1), so Y ~ U(0,1). Then E(X) = E(12Y) = 12(1/2) = 6.
tips: Recognise the normal kernel in x: (1/sqrt(2 pi y)) exp(-(x - 12y)^2/(2y)) is exactly the N(12y, y) density, so the conditional law is read off directly.
Because that kernel integrates to 1 for each y, the marginal of Y is the constant 1 on (0,1) - i.e. Y is Uniform(0,1). This identification drives all three parts.
Tower property: E(X) = E[E(X|Y)] = E(12Y). Never attempt the double integral directly.
E(Y) = 1/2, E(Y^2) = 1/3 and Var(Y) = 1/12 for U(0,1) - keep all three ready, since the next two parts need them.
solution: Write the joint density as f(x,y) = [1/sqrt(2 pi y)] exp(-(x - 12y)^2/(2y)) for -infinity < x < infinity and 0 < y < 1.
For fixed y this is exactly the N(12y, y) density in x, so X | Y = y ~ N(12y, y).
Integrating that normal density over x gives 1 for every y, so the marginal density of Y is 1 on (0,1), i.e. Y ~ Uniform(0,1).
By the tower property, E(X) = E[E(X | Y)] = E(12Y).
Hence option (d) is correct.

tips: Law of total variance: Var(X) = E[Var(X|Y)] + Var[E(X|Y)]. Both pieces are needed - dropping either gives 12 or 0.5, and option (c) 12 is planted for exactly that slip.
From X|Y ~ N(12Y, Y): the conditional variance is Y itself, whose expectation is 1/2; the conditional mean is 12Y, whose variance is 144 Var(Y).
Var(Y) = 1/12 for U(0,1), so 144(1/12) = 12 - the clean cancellation confirms the set-up.
The two contributions are of very different sizes here (0.5 versus 12), which is a useful reminder that the between-group term usually dominates.
solution: From the joint density, X | Y = y ~ N(12y, y) and Y ~ Uniform(0,1).
The law of total variance gives Var(X) = E[Var(X | Y)] + Var[E(X | Y)].
The conditional variance is Var(X | Y) = Y, so E[Var(X|Y)] = E(Y) = 1/2.
The conditional mean is E(X|Y) = 12Y, so Var[E(X|Y)] = 144 Var(Y) = 144(1/12) = 12.
Hence option (d) is correct.

tips: Condition first: E(XY) = E[E(XY|Y)] = E[Y E(X|Y)], because Y is fixed inside the inner expectation.
For U(0,1), E(Y^2) = 1/3 - not 1/4. Confusing E(Y^2) with [E(Y)]^2 gives 3 and a covariance of 0.
Reuse E(X) = 6 from the first part rather than recomputing; shared-stem items are built to chain.
Consistency check: Cov = 12 Var(Y) = 12/12 = 1, since X = 12Y plus conditional noise that is uncorrelated with Y - a neat one-line confirmation.
solution: From the joint density, X | Y = y ~ N(12y, y) and Y ~ Uniform(0,1), with E(X) = 6 from the earlier part.
Cov(X,Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y) = 4 - 3 = 1.
Equivalently Cov(X,Y) = Cov(12Y, Y) = 12 Var(Y) = 12/12 = 1. Option (a) is correct.

2023-Q11.shortcut: Y = 10 - X ~ Binomial(10, 3/4). The third cumulant of B(n,p) is npq(q-p) = 10(3/4)(1/4)(1/4 - 3/4) = -15/16.
tips: Reflection rule: X ~ B(n,p) implies n - X ~ B(n, 1-p). Apply it FIRST and then use the standard cumulant formula.
Third cumulant of the binomial: k3 = npq(q - p). It changes sign with the skewness, so p > 1/2 gives a negative value.
Here p = 3/4 exceeds q = 1/4, so q - p = -1/2 and the answer must be NEGATIVE - only option (a) qualifies.
Alternative route: cumulants of a reflected variable satisfy k3(c - X) = -k3(X). Since k3(X) = 10(1/4)(3/4)(1/2) = 15/16, the reflection gives -15/16.
solution: X ~ Binomial(10, 1/4), and Y = 10 - X counts the failures, so Y ~ Binomial(10, 3/4).
For Y the parameters are n = 10, p = 3/4 and q = 1/4.
The third cumulant of a binomial variable is k3 = n p q (q - p).
Equivalently, k3(10 - X) = -k3(X) = -10(1/4)(3/4)(3/4 - 1/4) = -15/16. Option (a) is correct.

2023-Q12.shortcut: The sum of three i.i.d. Exp(1) variables is Gamma(shape 3, rate 1); dividing by 3 multiplies the rate by 3, giving Gamma(n = 3, lambda = 3).
tips: Additive property: the sum of n i.i.d. Exp(lambda) variables is Gamma(shape n, rate lambda). Here the sum is Gamma(3, 1).
Scaling rule: if W ~ Gamma(shape a, rate b) then W/c ~ Gamma(shape a, rate bc). Dividing by 3 raises the rate from 1 to 3, leaving the shape unchanged.
The SHAPE never changes under scaling, so any answer with shape other than 3 - options (a) and (b), which are exponential, i.e. shape 1 - is wrong.
Check the mean: E of the average of three Exp(1) variables is 1, and Gamma(3, rate 3) has mean 3/3 = 1. Confirmed.
solution: X, Y, Z are i.i.d. Exponential(1), which is Gamma with shape 1 and rate 1.
By the additive property of the Gamma family with a common rate, X + Y + Z ~ Gamma(shape 3, rate 1).
Let W = X + Y + Z and consider W/3.
If W ~ Gamma(shape a, rate b), then W/c ~ Gamma(shape a, rate bc); with c = 3 and b = 1 the rate becomes 3.
Hence (X+Y+Z)/3 ~ Gamma with n = 3 and lambda = 3, whose mean is 3/3 = 1, agreeing with the mean of an average of Exp(1) variables.
Option (d) is correct.

2023-Q13.shortcut: Swap the order of summation: sum over n of s^(2n) sum over k <= n of p_k = sum over k of p_k sum over n >= k of s^(2n) = sum of p_k s^(2k)/(1-s^2) = P(s^2)/(1-s^2).
tips: Interchange the summations - the double sum over the region k <= n is the standard manoeuvre for turning a CDF generating function into a pmf one.
The inner geometric sum over n >= k gives s^(2k)/(1 - s^2), which supplies both the argument s^2 and the denominator.
The surviving sum of p_k (s^2)^k is by definition P(s^2), since P(t) = sum p_k t^k. Substituting the argument correctly is what separates the options.
Sanity check at s = 0: the left side is P(X <= 0) = p_0, and P(0)/(1-0) = p_0. Only options with argument s^2 or s pass, and the general identity settles it.
solution: Write P(X <= n) = sum over k = 0 to n of p_k, where p_k = P(X = k).
Then the required sum is S = sum over n >= 0 of s^(2n) sum over k = 0 to n of p_k.
Interchange the order of summation over the region 0 <= k <= n: S = sum over k >= 0 of p_k sum over n >= k of s^(2n).
The inner geometric series is s^(2k) + s^(2k+2) + ... = s^(2k)/(1 - s^2) for |s| < 1.
So S = [1/(1 - s^2)] sum over k >= 0 of p_k (s^2)^k = P(s^2)/(1 - s^2), since P(t) = E(t^X) = sum p_k t^k.
Hence option (c) is correct.

2023-Q14.shortcut: Interchanging sums, sum over x of x P(X > x) = sum over k of p_k [k(k-1)/2] = [E(X^2) - E(X)]/2. Doubling gives E(X^2) - E(X) = sigma^2 + mu^2 - mu.
tips: Swap the summations: sum over x of x sum over k > x of p_k = sum over k of p_k sum over x = 0 to k-1 of x, and the inner sum is k(k-1)/2.
The factor 2 outside is placed exactly to cancel the 1/2 from the triangular number - a strong hint that the identity is being tested.
Finish with E(X^2) = sigma^2 + mu^2, so the answer is sigma^2 + mu^2 - mu. Options (c) and (d) retain a stray 1/2.
Companion identity worth knowing: sum over x >= 0 of P(X > x) = E(X) for non-negative integer variables - the first-moment version of the same trick.
solution: Write S = sum over x >= 0 of x P(X > x) = sum over x >= 0 of x sum over k > x of p_k, where p_k = P(X = k).
Interchange the order of summation over the region 0 <= x < k: S = sum over k >= 0 of p_k sum over x = 0 to k-1 of x.
The inner sum is the triangular number k(k-1)/2.
So S = sum over k of p_k k(k-1)/2 = [E(X^2) - E(X)]/2.
Therefore 2S = E(X^2) - E(X).
Since E(X^2) = sigma^2 + mu^2 and E(X) = mu, the value is sigma^2 + mu^2 - mu, option (b).

2023-Q15.shortcut: The Y = 2 column has masses theta, 0, 2theta for X = -1, 0, 1, so the conditional probabilities are 1/3, 0, 2/3. The MGF is (e^(-t) + 2e^t)/3.
tips: For a conditional distribution, take only the relevant COLUMN and renormalise by its total - the value of theta never matters.
Column Y = 2 totals theta + 0 + 2theta = 3theta, so the weights are 1/3 and 2/3 on X = -1 and X = +1.
MGF = sum over x of e^(tx) P(X = x | Y = 2) = (1/3)e^(-t) + (2/3)e^t. Options (b) and (c) attach the weights to the wrong values.
Validity check: every MGF must equal 1 at t = 0. Here (1 + 2)/3 = 1, as required; option (b) gives 3/3 = 1 too, so use the weights, not this test, to choose.
solution: Summing the whole table: row X = -1 gives 8theta, row X = 0 gives 6theta and row X = 1 gives 6theta, a total of 20theta = 1, so theta = 1/20.
The column Y = 2 has entries theta at X = -1, 0 at X = 0 and 2theta at X = 1, totalling 3theta.
Conditional probabilities: P(X = -1 | Y = 2) = theta/3theta = 1/3, P(X = 0 | Y = 2) = 0, P(X = 1 | Y = 2) = 2theta/3theta = 2/3.
The moment generating function is M(t) = E(e^(tX) | Y = 2) = (1/3)e^(-t) + 0 + (2/3)e^t = (e^(-t) + 2e^t)/3.
Check M(0) = (1 + 2)/3 = 1. Option (a) is correct.

2023-Q16.shortcut: With conditional probabilities 1/3 on -1 and 2/3 on +1: E(X|Y=2) = 1/3 and E(X^2|Y=2) = 1, so the variance is 1 - 1/9 = 8/9.
tips: Since X takes only the values -1 and +1 here, X^2 = 1 with certainty, so E(X^2 | Y = 2) = 1 without any computation.
E(X|Y=2) = -1(1/3) + 1(2/3) = 1/3 - the same conditional distribution as the previous part, so reuse it.
Variance = 1 - (1/3)^2 = 8/9. Option (a) 1/3 is the conditional MEAN, the classic mis-selection.
A two-point variable on {-1, 1} with probability p on +1 has variance 4p(1-p) = 4(2/3)(1/3) = 8/9 - a fast cross-check.
solution: From the previous part, conditionally on Y = 2 the variable X takes the value -1 with probability 1/3 and +1 with probability 2/3.
Since X takes only the values -1 and +1 in this conditional distribution, X^2 = 1 always, so E(X^2 | Y = 2) = 1.
Equivalently, for a two-point variable on {-1, 1} with P(+1) = p, the variance is 4p(1-p) = 4(2/3)(1/3) = 8/9. Option (c) is correct.

2023-Q17.shortcut: Given Y = 2, the factor Y is the constant 2, so E(XY | Y = 2) = 2 E(X | Y = 2) = 2(1/3) = 2/3.
tips: Conditioning on Y = 2 makes Y a CONSTANT inside the expectation, so it can be pulled straight out - no joint computation is needed.
Reuse E(X | Y = 2) = 1/3 from the previous part; these three items are deliberately chained.
Option (b) 1/3 is E(X|Y=2) itself, the trap for candidates who forget to multiply by 2.
General rule: E(g(Y) h(X) | Y = y) = g(y) E(h(X) | Y = y) - worth stating as a formula, since it appears constantly.
solution: We condition on the event Y = 2, so within this conditional distribution Y takes the constant value 2.
Hence E(XY | Y = 2) = E(2X | Y = 2) = 2 E(X | Y = 2).
From the earlier parts, the conditional distribution of X given Y = 2 puts mass 1/3 on -1 and 2/3 on +1.
Therefore E(XY | Y = 2) = 2(1/3) = 2/3.
Option (c) is correct.

2023-Q18.shortcut: Integrating x first (substituting u = xy) gives B(13,7)/y^13; integrating that over y > 1 gives B(13,7)/12. So lambda = 12/B(13,7) = 19/B(12,7), since B(13,7) = (12/19)B(12,7).
tips: Beta second-kind integral: the integral from 0 to infinity of u^(m-1)/(1+u)^(m+n) du = B(m,n). With numerator power 12 and denominator power 20, m = 13 and n = 7.
The substitution u = xy turns (1 + xy) into (1 + u) and produces the factor y^(-13), which then integrates cleanly over (1, infinity) to 1/12.
Convert B(13,7) to B(12,7) using B(m,n) = Gamma(m)Gamma(n)/Gamma(m+n): the ratio B(13,7)/B(12,7) = 12/19, so lambda = 12 x 19/12 divided by B(12,7) = 19/B(12,7).
The options are all expressed in B(12,7), which is the signal that a Gamma-ratio conversion is expected - do it at the very end.
solution: Require the double integral of lambda x^12/(1+xy)^20 over x > 0, y > 1 to equal 1.
Inner integral over x: substitute u = xy, so x = u/y and dx = du/y, giving the integral of (u/y)^12/(1+u)^20 du/y = (1/y^13) times the integral of u^12/(1+u)^20 du.
That standard integral is B(m,n) with m - 1 = 12 and m + n = 20, i.e. B(13,7). So the inner integral equals B(13,7)/y^13.
Outer integral over y from 1 to infinity: the integral of y^(-13) dy = [y^(-12)/(-12)] from 1 to infinity = 1/12.
Hence lambda B(13,7)/12 = 1, giving lambda = 12/B(13,7).

2023-Q19.shortcut: Integrating out y gives f_X(x) = lambda x^11/[19(1+x)^19] = x^11/[B(12,7)(1+x)^19], the Beta second-kind density with m = 12 and n = 7.
tips: Beta type-II (second kind) density: f(x) = x^(m-1)/[B(m,n)(1+x)^(m+n)] on x > 0. Match the two exponents to read off m and n.
Here the numerator power is 11 so m = 12, and the denominator power is 19 so m + n = 19, giving n = 7.
Support decides the type: X ranges over (0, infinity), which is Beta type-II; Beta type-I lives on (0,1). That eliminates options (c) and (d) at once.
The substitution t = 1 + xy with y from 1 to infinity makes t run from 1 + x to infinity, which is what produces the (1+x)^(-19) factor.
solution: The marginal of X is f_X(x) = the integral over y from 1 to infinity of lambda x^12/(1 + xy)^20 dy.
Substitute t = 1 + xy, so dt = x dy and y = 1 corresponds to t = 1 + x, with t running to infinity.
f_X(x) = lambda x^12 times the integral from 1+x to infinity of t^(-20) dt/x = lambda x^11 [t^(-19)/19] evaluated at t = 1 + x = lambda x^11/[19(1+x)^19].
With lambda = 19/B(12,7), this becomes f_X(x) = x^11/[B(12,7)(1 + x)^19] for x > 0.
The Beta distribution of the second kind with parameters (m, n) has density x^(m-1)/[B(m,n)(1+x)^(m+n)]; matching gives m - 1 = 11 and m + n = 19, so m = 12 and n = 7.
Hence X follows a Beta Type-II distribution with parameters (12, 7), option (a).

2023-Q20.shortcut: The x-integral computed earlier gives B(13,7)/y^13, so f_Y(y) = lambda B(13,7)/y^13 = 12/y^13 on y > 1.
tips: Reuse the inner integral from the normalisation step: it already equals B(13,7)/y^13, so only the constant lambda needs attaching.
lambda B(13,7) = 12 exactly, because lambda was chosen to make the whole double integral 1 and the y-integral of y^(-13) is 1/12.
Validity check: the integral of 12 y^(-13) over (1, infinity) is 12/12 = 1. Options (a), (b) and (c) integrate to 1 as well, so use the derivation rather than this test.
This is a Pareto density with shape 12 on (1, infinity) - recognising the family makes the exponent pairing (12, 13) easy to remember.
solution: The marginal of Y is f_Y(y) = the integral over x from 0 to infinity of lambda x^12/(1 + xy)^20 dx.
As computed in the normalisation step, substituting u = xy gives this integral as lambda B(13,7)/y^13 for y > 1.
From the normalisation, lambda B(13,7)/12 = 1, so lambda B(13,7) = 12.
Hence f_Y(y) = 12/y^13 for y > 1, and 0 otherwise.
Check: the integral of 12 y^(-13) dy from 1 to infinity = 12 [y^(-12)/(-12)] from 1 to infinity = 1, a valid density.
Option (d) is correct.
